title: Eli and His Sons
subtitle: Knowing the truth and failing to act
lesson:
God’s charge against Eli was that he knew what his sons were doing and failed to restrain them. His words of objection did not fulfil every duty of his office. Spiritual responsibility calls for a response appropriate to the authority and knowledge a person has.

The ark could not be used to secure victory while the people ignored God’s word. Worship, office and religious association cannot make persistent wrongdoing acceptable.
question: What did Eli know, what did he say, and what did God say he had failed to do?
story: At Shiloh, people brought offerings to worship the Lord. Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, treated those offerings with contempt. They demanded meat before the proper offering had been made, and their servants threatened force when worshippers objected. Scripture also records their sexual misconduct with women serving at the tabernacle entrance.

Eli heard what was happening. He rebuked his sons and warned them about sinning against the Lord, but they would not listen. A man of God announced judgment against the household. Later the Lord confirmed the warning to Samuel, explaining that Eli knew about the wickedness and had not restrained his sons.

When Israel was defeated by the Philistines, the elders decided to bring the ark of the covenant into the camp. Hophni and Phinehas accompanied it. The people greeted its arrival with a great shout. They had brought a sacred object into the battle, but they had not dealt with their disobedience.

Israel was defeated again. Eli’s sons died and the ark was captured. When a messenger brought the news to Eli, the mention of the ark caused him to fall backward from his seat. He broke his neck and died. Phinehas’s wife also heard the news. As she gave birth and died, she named her child Ichabod, speaking of the departure of glory.

The account began with wrongdoing in a place of worship and with a leader who knew about it. It ended with consequences that rank, family ties and sacred objects could not prevent. Samuel’s growing faithfulness alongside this decline shows a different way to respond to responsibility before God.

title: David Nathan and Solomon
subtitle: Repentance mercy and consequences
lesson:
David used royal power to conceal sin at another person’s expense. Nathan’s confrontation shows that position cannot remove responsibility before God. Confession begins by accepting the truth rather than trying to control appearances.

Forgiveness did not make every consequence disappear. God’s later love for Solomon reveals mercy and continuing purpose, but it does not call the earlier adultery and killing good.
question: How did David’s efforts to hide his sin lead to further harm, and how did Nathan confront him?
story: David remained in Jerusalem while his army fought the Ammonites. From his roof he saw Bathsheba bathing. He learned that she was Uriah’s wife, sent for her and committed adultery with her. When she later told him she was pregnant, he began trying to conceal what he had done.

David brought Uriah home from the battlefield and encouraged him to go to his house. Uriah would not enjoy its comforts while the ark, Israel and his fellow soldiers were in temporary quarters. Even after David made him drunk, he did not go home. His conduct frustrated the king’s plan.

David sent a letter to Joab through Uriah himself. It ordered that Uriah be placed in dangerous fighting and that support be withdrawn. Uriah died. After Bathsheba’s mourning, David brought her into his house as his wife. The account says that what David had done displeased the Lord.

God sent Nathan with a story about a rich man who took a poor man’s treasured lamb. David condemned the man. Nathan then identified David as the guilty one and exposed the wrong he had tried to hide. David acknowledged his sin against the Lord. Nathan announced forgiveness, but also declared consequences.

The child became ill. David pleaded and fasted, but the child died. Later Bathsheba bore Solomon, whom the Lord loved. The account holds David’s guilt, God’s forgiveness, painful consequences and God’s continuing purpose together. It does not allow the king to use later mercy as an excuse for the earlier wrong.

title: The Prophet Who Turned Back
subtitle: When a spiritual claim contradicts God’s word
lesson:
The narrative explicitly says that the older prophet lied. His office and his claim about an angel did not make his report trustworthy or cancel the instruction already given. Spiritual teaching should be tested by Scripture, rather than accepted solely because of a title or an impressive experience.

The account is a particular judgment narrative. It warns us to hold to God’s word, without authorising private threats of disaster against people who disagree with us.
question: Why did the man of God refuse the king’s invitation but accept the older prophet’s, and what should have remained decisive?
story: A man of God came from Judah to Bethel and spoke against the altar where Jeroboam stood. The king stretched out his hand to order his arrest, and his hand withered. The altar was torn apart as the announced sign had said. At Jeroboam’s request, the man of God prayed, and the king’s hand was restored.

The king invited him home for refreshment and a reward. He refused. The Lord had told him not to eat bread or drink water there and not to return by the way he had come. He left by a different route, resisting both royal pressure and the offered reward.

An older prophet heard about the events and followed him. He found him resting beneath an oak and invited him home. The visitor repeated the command he had received. The older man then claimed that an angel had instructed him to bring the visitor back to eat. Scripture plainly states that he was lying.

The man from Judah returned and ate. During the meal, a true word of judgment came through the prophet who had deceived him. He had disobeyed the instruction he knew. After he left, a lion killed him. The lion and the donkey remained beside the body, and the lion did not eat it or attack the donkey.

The older prophet recovered the body and mourned. He also affirmed that the announced word against Bethel would come to pass. The original instruction had not changed simply because another religious voice had contradicted it.
